Clearly show the cliff edge and rock layers, the suspended human figure, taut harness lines, a fully inflated canopy, wind or motion cues, and distant landscape depth. Compose the scene so the relationship between height, danger, and safe descent is immediately readable. Put strong emphasis on dynamic scale, clear silhouette, atmospheric depth, and polished editorial illustration.

history.critique: Brief & Intent: The cliff is present but its rock layers are nearly invisible — faint low-contrast horizontals on a flat dark slab — so 'clearly show the cliff edge and rock layers' is only half met. Worse, the rider floats in open center-left sky, far from the rock, so the core 'descending BESIDE a dramatic cliff' relationship and the height/danger/safe-descent reading are diluted; the figure reads as a generic parachute over mountains rather than a knife-edge escape. The suspended human is a tiny dark blob: legs are two thick sticks, the torso is an unreadable mass, so the 'clear silhouette' emphasis fails at this scale. Wind cues are scattered random white dashes with no coherent direction or flow. Clarity & Hierarchy: Four anchors compete — the large serif title, the orange canopy, the top-right legend, and the bottom-left telemetry — so the canopy (the intended hero) never wins. The legend is a crutch that explains the obvious (orange = canopy) and sits as UI noise over the cliff. A real correctness bug: the altitude bar's axis tops out at 2,000 m but the readout is 2,086 m, so the marker overflows its own scale. The 'HOLD SPACE / RELEASE / RESET' controls are low-contrast and orphaned in the corner, implying interactivity that the static frame doesn't confirm. Visual System & Craft: The canopy's 'highlights' are hard-edged light-orange rectangles that read as janky patches, not shaped light on a dome; the underside/rim is flat so 'fully inflated' is weak. A stray faint arc among the risers breaks the taut-line read. The cliff's cream edge glow is slightly too thick, and the interior lacks layered tonal bands. The horizon haze is a soft-edged smear that looks like a smudge rather than atmospheric depth, and the purple ridges are flat single-tone polygons. Expressiveness & Distinctiveness: The 'field atlas / Plate 07' editorial frame is genuinely distinctive and the palette is cohesive, but the scene itself is generic — the dramatic cliff is underused as a passive side panel, there is no strong diagonal or directional pull, and the danger the brief demands is not felt. Real trade-offs: keeping the cliff as a clean right-hand panel preserves the tidy plate composition but sacrifices the intimacy and peril of 'beside the cliff'; the legend and telemetry add 'system' credibility but tax the hero; enlarging the rider would fix the silhouette but risks breaking realistic scale against the canopy.
history.suggestion: One prioritized plan that keeps every required element (cliff edge + strata, suspended figure, taut lines, inflated canopy, wind cues, distant depth, height/danger/safe readability, dynamic scale, silhouette, atmospheric depth, editorial polish) and stays fully self-contained SVG: (1) Re-anchor the cliff as the danger axis — extend it to dominate the right third, build the rock from 4–6 higher-contrast alternating strata bands plus a few fault lines, add a bright knife-edge ridge at the top where the rider 'eased off,' and shift the rider's flight line rightward so the canopy nearly grazes the edge; this single move restores 'beside the cliff,' height, and danger without crowding the title. (2) Fix the silhouette: scale the rider up modestly, give it a confident solid dark shape with a thin warm rim-light on the canopy-facing side, and redraw the harness as a clean symmetric V of taut risers with a visible chest strap — delete the stray arc and fan the lines evenly so 'taut' reads instantly. (3) Replace the random dashes with a coherent wind system: 3–5 curved flow lines sweeping off the cliff face outward and down, aligned to the descent vector, plus two short speed streaks trailing the canopy, so motion has direction and ties the figure to the rock. (4) Canopy craft: swap the rectangular highlights for curved crescents that follow the dome, add a darker shaded underside/rim to sell inflation, and tilt the canopy a few degrees to imply drift. (5) Rebalance hierarchy: demote the legend to a single small footnote row (or remove it), keep the title as the secondary anchor, and fix the telemetry by rescaling the altitude axis to 0–2,500 m (or correcting the value) so bar and number agree; fold the SPACE/RELEASE hints into the telemetry panel at higher contrast. (6) Deepen atmosphere: convert the haze smear into a true vertical gradient band, add a third, lighter distant ridge for more depth, and let the warm sun glow sit in the gap between cliff and mountains to backlight the scene. Sequence matters: do (1) and (2) first because they resolve the brief's core readability and the silhouette emphasis; (3)–(4) then strengthen craft and motion; (5)–(6) finalize hierarchy and depth.
